result:
I'll write about something that's been on my mind lately: the strange, quiet intimacy of watching someone choose fruit at the grocery store.

There's a particular stillness to the produce section that I've grown to love, a kind of meditative hush beneath the fluorescent hum. People move differently among vegetables. They slow down. They touch things. In a world of digital transactions and automated checkout, the produce section remains stubbornly, beautifully analog. You have to use your hands. You have to make judgments with your eyes and your nose and the subtle give of pressure against your thumb. There's no algorithm for ripeness, not really. You have to decide for yourself.

I watch a woman in her sixties examining avocados. She picks one up, holds it to the light as if checking for contraband, then sets it down with the gentleness of someone placing a sleeping baby in a crib. She tries another. Her fingers spread across the dark skin like she's reading braille. I wonder what she's making. Guacamole for a family gathering, perhaps. A salad for one. Maybe she's developed this careful ritual over decades of disappointing avocados, the ones that turned out brown and stringy inside, the ones that promised creaminess and delivered only regret. Each avocado is a small gamble. She's learned to read the odds.

The man beside her is less patient. He grabs three tomatoes in quick succession, barely looking, and drops them into his basket. I find myself judging him, which is absurd. Maybe he's cooked ten thousand meals and knows exactly what he needs. Maybe he's in a hurry because someone's waiting. Maybe the tomatoes don't matter to him the way they matter to me, the way I turn each one to find the bruise hidden against the stem, the way I hold them to my face to smell that particular green-gold scent of summer even in December.

I think about my grandmother, who could tell you the exact day a peach would reach its peak. She grew up during the Depression, when fruit was precious, when a bad choice meant waste you couldn't afford. She passed some of this to my mother, who passed less to me, and I wonder what my own children will know about choosing food. Whether they'll stand in grocery stores feeling vaguely anxious about all the things they never learned, or whether the future will solve this problem entirely, delivering perfect produce to their doors, ripeness guaranteed, all the uncertainty engineered away.

There's something lost in that efficiency, though I couldn't tell you exactly what. Maybe it's the way uncertainty forces presence. When you're not sure if the melon is good, you have to pay attention. You have to be there, in your body, using senses that have nothing to do with screens. The cantaloupe's rough netting under your palm. The hollow sound when you thump it. The sweet, almost fermented smell at the blossom end. These are ancient negotiations between human and nature, even here under artificial light, even with produce shipped from countries I'll never visit.

I select my own items slowly, perhaps too slowly. A woman waiting for the bunches of kale catches my eye and smiles with what I choose to interpret as solidarity rather than impatience. We're both doing this strange, old thing. We're both trusting ourselves to know what good food looks like, feels like, despite years of industrial agriculture designed to make everything uniform, everything predictable, everything exactly the same from Maine to California.

The paradox of modern grocery shopping is that abundance itself has become a kind of poverty. We have twelve kinds of apples in October, but none of them taste like the apples I remember from my grandfather's tree, the ones with brown spots and inconsistent sizes and flavor so intense it made your gums ache. We've traded specificity for availability, seasonality for convenience. I can have a strawberry in January, but it will be a pale imitation of itself, a strawberry playing dress-up, all color and no taste.

Still, I find moments of genuine pleasure here. The discovery of a perfect fig, soft as a sigh, the interior like jam held barely in place. The weight of a good pomegranate, heavy with hidden jewels. Even the humble potato, when you find the right one, firm and unblemished, promising transformation through heat and salt and butter.

I think about all the hands that touched these things before mine. The pickers in fields I can't imagine, starting before dawn. The truck drivers crossing states. The stockers working overnight, filling these bins while the city sleeps. My careful selection is the end of a long chain of human effort, most of it invisible, most of it underpaid. I try to choose well partly out of respect for that labor. Wasting food feels like a kind of violence against this hidden network of care.

At the checkout, the young man scans my items without looking at them. The figs pass over the laser, beep, become numbers. The tomatoes, the kale, the single perfect avocado I finally found. I want to tell him about the woman reading avocados like braille, about my grandmother's peaches, about the particular loneliness of January strawberries. But the transaction doesn't allow for this. The conveyor belt moves forward. Someone behind me clears their throat.

In the parking lot, I set my bags in the trunk with the same care the woman used with her avocados. I drive home through streets going dark, carrying food I chose with my hands, with my imperfect knowledge, with some part of me that still believes I can tell what's good by touching it, smelling it, holding it to the light.

Tonight I'll make something simple. A salad, probably. I'll slice the figs and watch their dark centers open like small flowers. I'll taste one standing at the counter, before anything else, and for a moment I'll be completely present, completely in my body, grateful for this small, daily miracle of choosing and being chosen, of hunger and its quiet, necessary satisfaction.
